title: How do you add distributed tracing to a gRPC microservice (client/server interceptors injecting/extracting trace context, Jaeger/Zipkin/OpenTelemetry)?
shortTitle: How do you add distributed tracing to a gRPC microservice (client/server interceptors injecting/extracting trace context, Jaeger/Zipkin/OpenTelemetry)?

s1_definition.profdef: Distributed tracing follows a single request as it flows across multiple services, recording a tree of spans under one trace id. In gRPC you implement it with interceptors: a client interceptor injects the current trace context (trace id, span id, sampling flags) into the call's metadata, and a server interceptor extracts that context and starts a child span, continuing the trace. The standard approach uses OpenTelemetry for instrumentation and context propagation (via the W3C traceparent format) and exports spans to a backend like Jaeger or Zipkin for visualization. Each service becomes a span in the overall trace, so you can see end-to-end latency and failures across the chain.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a single transfer request at National Bank of India passing through several departments. Distributed tracing is like attaching one tracking number to Rajesh's request and stamping a timestamped slip every time it enters and leaves a department. The client interceptor is the clerk who writes the tracking number onto the envelope before sending it (inject), and the server interceptor is the receiving clerk who reads that number and keeps using it (extract). At the end, a tracing tool like Jaeger assembles all the stamps into one timeline, so you can see exactly which department was slow or where the request failed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use a client interceptor to inject trace context into gRPC metadata and a server interceptor to extract it and start a child span, with OpenTelemetry propagating the trace and Jaeger or Zipkin visualizing it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Distributed tracing follows a single request as it flows across multiple services, recording a tree of spans under one trace id. In gRPC you implement it with interceptors: a client interceptor injects the current trace context (trace id, span id, sampling flags) into the call's metadata, and a server interceptor extracts that context and starts a child span, continuing the trace. The standard approach uses OpenTelemetry for instrumentation and context propagation (via the W3C traceparent format) and exports spans to a backend like Jaeger or Zipkin for visualization. Each service becomes a span in the overall trace, so you can see end-to-end latency and failures across the chain.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a single transfer request at National Bank of India passing through several departments. Distributed tracing is like attaching one tracking number to Rajesh's request and stamping a timestamped slip every time it enters and leaves a department. The client interceptor is the clerk who writes the tracking number onto the envelope before sending it (inject), and the server interceptor is the receiving clerk who reads that number and keeps using it (extract). At the end, a tracing tool like Jaeger assembles all the stamps into one timeline, so you can see exactly which department was slow or where the request failed.

**One line to remember:** Use a client interceptor to inject trace context into gRPC metadata and a server interceptor to extract it and start a child span, with OpenTelemetry propagating the trace and Jaeger or Zipkin visualizing it.

sections.s2_technical:
A trace is identified by a trace id shared across all services for one logical request, and each unit of work is a span with its own span id and a parent span id, forming a tree. For tracing to span services, the trace context must travel with the request. In gRPC that carrier is the call metadata (gRPC's equivalent of headers). The client side injects the active context into metadata before the call leaves, and the server side extracts it from incoming metadata and makes it the parent of a new server span. The modern standard format is W3C traceparent, carried in a metadata key, and OpenTelemetry handles the inject and extract through its propagators so you do not hand-roll the serialization.

Concretely, you add a gRPC `ClientInterceptor` that, on each call, asks the OpenTelemetry propagator to inject the current span context into a `Metadata` object attached to the outgoing call. You add a `ServerInterceptor` that, on each incoming call, extracts the context from the received `Metadata`, starts a server span as a child, and makes it current for the duration of the handler. In practice you rarely write these by hand because OpenTelemetry ships a ready-made gRPC instrumentation that registers both interceptors for you; you just add the agent or the library and configure the exporter. You then configure an exporter, for example OTLP to an OpenTelemetry Collector that forwards to Jaeger, or a direct Jaeger or Zipkin exporter, plus a sampler to control how many traces are recorded.

The payoff is end-to-end visibility: a trace shows the transfer service span, nested under it the account service span, nested under that the ledger or database span, each with timing, so you immediately see which hop caused latency or where an error occurred. Senior nuances: propagate context correctly across async boundaries and thread pools, because the active context is thread-local and must be captured and restored when work hops threads; choose a sampling strategy (head-based probability sampling, or tail-based in the collector) to balance cost and coverage; enrich spans with attributes like account type or amount bucket, but never put sensitive PII or raw account numbers and balances into span attributes in a banking system; correlate traces with logs by injecting the trace id into the logging MDC so a log line links to its trace; and keep tracing overhead low by batching span exports. Combining gRPC metadata propagation, OpenTelemetry, and a Jaeger backend gives a complete, standards-based tracing setup.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A transfer at National Bank of India touches the transfer service, the account service, and the ledger, and sometimes it is slow, but no one can tell which hop is responsible. This is exactly what distributed tracing solves — one trace id across all hops shows where time is spent.

Problem 2 — The trace context must pass automatically between gRPC services without changing business code. This is exactly what client and server interceptors plus OpenTelemetry propagation provide — inject on the client, extract on the server.

The demo registers an OpenTelemetry-style client interceptor that injects trace context into metadata and a server interceptor that extracts it and starts a child span, then exports to Jaeger. Classes and steps: `TracingClientInterceptor` (inject), `TracingServerInterceptor` (extract + child span), `OtelConfig` (tracer + Jaeger exporter), and wiring into the channel and server.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run with OpenTelemetry Java agent (auto-instruments gRPC — no code change):
java -javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar \
     -Dotel.service.name=transfer-service \
     -Dotel.exporter.otlp.endpoint=http://otel-collector:4317 \
     -jar target/grpc-tracing-service-1.0.0.jar

# View traces in Jaeger UI (http://localhost:16686)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer request from Rajesh that flows transfer service to account service.

Step 1 — The transfer service starts a root span for the incoming request, generating a trace id and a span id.

Step 2 — When the transfer service calls the account service over gRPC, the `TracingClientInterceptor` injects the active trace context as a W3C traceparent value into the call metadata, so the trace id and the current span id ride along with the request.

Step 3 — The account service's `TracingServerInterceptor` extracts that context from the incoming metadata and starts a new server span whose parent is the transfer service's span, continuing the same trace. It logs the shared trace id.

Step 4 — Both spans are exported by the batch processor to the OTLP collector, which forwards them to Jaeger. In the Jaeger UI the transfer span and the nested account span appear under one trace with timings, so an engineer can see exactly which hop was slow or failed.

```
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [FINE] Injected trace context into bank.AccountService/Transfer
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Server span started traceId=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736
2026-10-26 14:55:11 [INFO] Transfer processed; span exported to Jaeger
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — gRPC Tracing Interceptors ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Interceptor/Decorator: Client+Server interceptors wrap calls   │
  │    WHY: add tracing without touching business code             │
  │ Context Propagation: W3C traceparent in gRPC metadata          │
  │    WHY: one trace id flows across all hops                     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: each interceptor does only inject or only extract           │
  │ O: new backend = new exporter config, no code change           │
  │ D: interceptors depend on OpenTelemetry API, not Jaeger directly│
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. transfer service root span (traceId generated)
  2.   → ClientInterceptor.inject(context → metadata traceparent)
  3.   → Account ServerInterceptor.extract(metadata) → child span
  4.   → span.end() → BatchSpanProcessor → OTLP → Jaeger
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Distributed tracing follows one request across many services by recording a tree of spans under a single trace id, and in gRPC I implement it with interceptors. On the client side an interceptor injects the active trace context, the trace id and span id in W3C traceparent format, into the call's metadata, which is gRPC's equivalent of headers. On the server side an interceptor extracts that context from the incoming metadata and starts a new server span as a child of the caller's span, continuing the same trace. I use OpenTelemetry to handle the inject and extract through its propagators and to export spans, and I send them to a backend like Jaeger or Zipkin to visualize the end-to-end timeline.

In practice I rarely hand-write these interceptors because OpenTelemetry ships ready-made gRPC instrumentation, often via a Java agent, that registers both interceptors automatically, so I just add the agent and configure the OTLP exporter and a sampler. The sampler lets me control how many traces I record to balance cost against coverage.

In my banking work at National Bank of India this gave us real end-to-end visibility. A transfer request starts a root span in the transfer service, the client interceptor injects the context when it calls the account service, the account service's server interceptor extracts it and starts a child span, and the same continues down to the ledger. In Jaeger the whole thing appears as one trace with nested spans and timings, so when a transfer is slow I can immediately see which hop is responsible instead of guessing.

The senior points I always add are to propagate context correctly across async boundaries and thread pools, because the active context is thread-local and must be captured and restored when work hops threads; to never put sensitive data like raw account numbers or balances into span attributes in a banking system; and to inject the trace id into the logging MDC so every log line links back to its trace. So my summary answer is: a client interceptor injects trace context into gRPC metadata, a server interceptor extracts it and opens a child span, OpenTelemetry propagates the trace with W3C traceparent, and Jaeger or Zipkin shows the full request path for fast, precise diagnosis.
